                                           PROJECT NO. 58481
    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT
                                                       §                     BEFORE THE
    LARGE LOAD
                                                       §             PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS
                                                       §                      OF TEXAS
    UNDER PURA §37.0561


    COMMENTS OF THE ADVANCED POWER ALLIANCE AND AMERICAN CLEAN
                        POWER ASSOCIATION

        The Advanced Power Alliance and American Clean Power Association file these joint

comments on the Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Proposal for Publication of

a proposed new 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.194 relating to Large Load

Interconnection Standards. This proposed rule will implement Public Utility Regulatory Act

(PURA) §37.0561, as enacted by Senate Bill (SB) 6 during the Texas 89th Regular Legislative

Session. The new rule will implement new PURA §37.0561, which requires the commission to

establish standards for interconnecting large load customers in the ERCOT power region in a

manner designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the potential for

stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.



                                                  I. INTRODUCTION

        The Advanced Power Alliance (APA) and the American Clean Power Association (ACP)

serve as the voice1 of a diverse cross-section of the world’s leading energy companies, energy

investors, energy consumers, and power generation manufacturers from across the clean power

sector that are driving high-tech innovation through the development of generation assets including

wind, solar, and energy storage, spurring massive investment in the U.S. economy, including a


1
 The views and recommendations contained in this filing reflect the position of the Advanced Power Alliance in its
capacity as a trade organization representing a diverse membership. They should not be construed to represent the
unanimous views of all individual member companies.

                                                         1
 cumulative investment in Texas of $173 billion to date, while creating jobs for American workers,

including more than 125,800 in Texas alone.2 Projects developed by our member companies and

investors generate more than $859.2 million state and local tax dollars for schools, services, and

infrastructure, as well multi-generational income for Texas landowners—more than $887.5 million

annually—mainly in rural Texas.3 Our members’ projects help reduce Texans’ electricity costs

and create cleaner air, water, and improved human health.



                                          II. GENERAL COMMENTS

       We appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the Commission’s Proposal for

Publication regarding Large Load Interconnection Standards. As Texas continues to attract

significant industrial investment, including data centers and advanced manufacturing,

establishing a predictable and commercially viable interconnection framework is essential for

maintaining both grid reliability and economic competitiveness.

       While we support the Commission’s goal of reducing speculative requests and protecting

the ERCOT system from stranded costs, the current proposal imposes a premature and untenable

financial obligation for developers by requiring non-refundable financial commitments before

either MW allocation or cost responsibility is known. Specifically, the proposed rule requires

non-refundable financial commitments at the Intermediate Agreement stage before a developer

has certainty regarding its megawatt (MW) allocation from ERCOT or its ultimate cost

responsibility, which is currently being debated in Project No. 58484.




2
  Texas Clean Energy Fact Sheet, American Clean Power Association, December 2025.
https://cleanpower.org/facts/state-fact-
sheets/#:~:text=The%20clean%20power%20industry%20is,bottom%20of%20the%20text%20box.
3
  Ibid.

                                                2
        These comments focus on five critical areas that require refinement to align the proposal

with the cost-causation principles embedded in the Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA):

       Financial Security Requirements: Ensuring that security deposits serve as risk-
       mitigation tools rather than punitive penalties, particularly when project delays or
       capacity denials are outside the developer’s control.
       Intermediate Agreement Security Structure: Refining subsection (g) to ensure the
       framework does not result in premature capital forfeiture before developers have
       visibility into project viability.
       Interconnection Agreement Stage Fees: Clarifying that additional $/MW fees at the
       Interconnection Agreement stage are unnecessary and duplicative given existing security
       postings and CIAC obligations.
       Site Control and Development Timing: Adjusting site control and execution timelines
       to reflect the realities of project financing and land acquisition.
       Regulatory Certainty: Providing clear grandfathering provisions for projects with
       existing Interconnection Agreements to prevent duplicative costs and unnecessary re-
       study exposure.


   By adopting the refinements recommended below, the Commission can implement a standard

that discourages speculation without inadvertently stifling commercially viable, capital-intensive

large-load projects that are vital to the Texas economy.



                       III.    FINANCIAL SECURITY REQUIREMENTS

       Experience across FERC-jurisdictional ISOs/RTOs demonstrates that well-designed

financial security requirements, paired with proportionate withdrawal penalties, are effective in

discouraging speculative or commercially non-viable interconnection requests. Increasing

security obligations at successive stages of the study process appropriately encourages

developers to withdraw earlier, thereby reducing late-stage terminations that can trigger costly

delays and restudies. Further, tying security amounts to a developer’s identified cost

responsibility, once established, ensures that each interconnecting entity bears the direct cost




                                                 3
 consequences of its actual system impacts. This approach incentivizes timely withdrawal by

projects whose upgrades would impose disproportionate or uneconomic costs on the system.

       Once Interconnection Agreements are executed, financial security serves as the funding

mechanism for interconnection facilities and network upgrades in the event an interconnection

customer withdraws but upgrades are still needed by remaining projects in the cluster.

Importantly, these securities should remain “at-risk” only to the extent necessary to cover actual

underfunded upgrades or restudies caused directly by developer withdrawals. If the load

proceeds as expected, security should be refunded promptly once the load reaches commercial

operation. This approach ensures that security payments remain limited to the system impacts

attributable to the interconnecting entity and aligns with fundamental cost-causation principles

embedded in PURA.



              IV.    INTERMEDIATE AGREEMENT SECURITY STRUCTURE

       The Proposal for Publication does not adequately limit a developer’s financial exposure

to its actual impact on the transmission system. At the Intermediate Agreement stage, a $/MW

security requirement is reasonable as a placeholder because upgrade costs and MW allocations

are not yet known. However, the proposed $50,000/MW security, of which 80% is non-

refundable, is excessive and punitive given the developer’s lack of visibility into final upgrade

costs or confirmed MW allocation.

       When a large load signs the Intermediate Agreement, it must post the full $50,000/MW

despite knowing neither its MW allocation nor its upgrade costs. Although the proposed rule

does not explicitly label this security as “non-refundable,” the mechanics of subsection (g)

ensure that only 20% is actually refundable. This results in a forfeited penalty if the project does



                                                  4
 not proceed for any reason beyond the developer’s control. This is particularly problematic

because loads in the batch study process may be denied full capacity and therefore will have no

opportunity to avoid the forfeiture of $40,000/MW, effectively an 80% penalty.

       A developer should not be required to forfeit $40,000/MW simply because a study

determines that resulting costs are commercially non-viable or ERCOT is unable to provide the

requested MW allocation. Subjecting Intermediate Agreements to subsection (g) effectively

creates a non-refundable punitive fee for every load that is partially or wholly denied capacity by

the system, withdraws during the commitment period, or fails to meet 100% of peak demand

within six months of the energization schedule, even when delays are attributable to the utility or

supply chain issues and are outside the developer’s control. This creates unacceptable risk and

will make obtaining such security instruments from lenders extremely expensive and potentially

unworkable.

       To create a more balanced and commercially reasonable process, we recommend

reducing the initial security requirement to the $10,000–$20,000/MW range. To reflect the risk

of restudies and cost uncertainty, no more than 10% of this amount should be non-refundable,

with the remainder refunded if the developer’s withdrawal does not adversely affect other

requests in the cluster. The non-refundable portion should be held until the end of the study

process and used only to fund underfunded upgrades or restudies. Any unused portion should be

refunded.

       Because ERCOT’s batch study process introduces uncertainty in both upgrade costs and

MW allocation, security should be fully refundable if the developer receives a substantially

smaller allocation than requested. A request receiving no MW allocation is no longer

commercially viable and, by definition, does not impact the cluster. Alternatively, the



                                                 5
 Commission should allow developers to transfer security associated with unallocated MW into

the subsequent batch. The Commission should consider a one-time transfer mechanism such as

the one used in SPP’s Consolidated Planning Process.4

           Additionally, significant uncertainty exists regarding the transmission costs that may

ultimately be assigned to large loads due to the pending transmission cost allocation rule in

Project No. 58484. It is premature to impose non-refundable penalties while the Commission is

still evaluating whether PUCT Staff recommendations regarding large loads paying for costs

traditionally classified as system upgrades will be adopted, as this represents a major departure

from current practice. Multiple parties, including utilities, have expressed concern that such costs

are nearly impossible to allocate accurately to specific loads. This uncertainty further

underscores the need to correct the subsection (g) reference for Intermediate Agreements, as

loads withdrawing prematurely would be penalized despite lacking knowledge of their ultimate

capacity allocation or economic viability.



                        V.       INTERCONNECTION AGREEMENT STAGE FEES

           If the Commission’s intent is to allocate costs to load requests based on their contribution

to system needs, an additional $/MW fee at the Interconnection Agreement stage is unnecessary.

At this point, the developer is already financially committed through security for significant

equipment, security for system upgrades, and Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC).

Requiring 100% of expected costs upfront and making security non-refundable already mitigates

the risk of stranded costs. Adding another non-refundable fee would only create a barrier to

market entry and may encourage large loads to locate outside of ERCOT.



4
    SPP Tariff, Attachment AY, Section V.3.2, etariff.ferc.gov.

                                                             6
         There is also concern with the proposal to retain a fixed percentage of security for

projects that withdraw after executing an Interconnection Agreement or that fail to meet 100% of

their energization schedule within six months. Security should be collected in an amount

sufficient to cover costs caused by the load, and any remainder should be returned to the

developer. Converting security into a penalty for missing deadlines in an uncertain environment,

particularly given global supply chain instability, will create unfair outcomes and significantly

increase the cost of obtaining security. At a minimum, there must be a cure period and

consideration of cause, including delays attributable to utilities or third-party vendors.

        Commission Staff’s Draft Evaluation of Transmission Cost Recovery correctly observes

that extending interconnection cost allocation to “highway” system upgrades presents

challenges.5 Cost allocation becomes a modeling exercise where small changes can significantly

shift assigned costs. In large clusters, this increases the risk of restudies and unexpected cost

increases, as each change affects the entire cluster. This dynamic has contributed to

interconnection delays in other ISOs/RTOs across the country and is one reason ERCOT has

historically interconnected generation more efficiently than other regions.

        Furthermore, costs charged under subsections (g) and (h) apply to equipment or services

that cannot be “completely canceled.” While some sunk costs should be borne by the load that

caused them, utilities should not charge developers for equipment that is subsequently reused for

another project. Given long equipment lead times, a withdrawal may not delay interconnection

for another developer, and capacity may be reassigned. In such cases, at least a portion of the

attributed investment should be reallocated rather than charged entirely to the withdrawing load

to avoid utility over-recovery.


5
 Staff Memo and Draft Report w/ April 13 Comment Deadline. Project No. 58484. Posted March 16, 2026. Pages
42-43. 58484_77_1603622.PDF.

                                                     7
        If the Commission prefers an interconnection fee in lieu of assigning “highway” upgrade

costs directly, the fee should reflect the broader benefits large loads receive from the

transmission system. The fee should be based on a structured, transparent, and stakeholder-vetted

analysis rather than an arbitrary value. SPP’s proposal to incorporate large load interconnections

into its Consolidated Planning Process provides a useful example: large loads pay an upfront

$/MW fee based on their share of transmission portfolio costs or potential stranded costs,

assessed through economic benefits, power-flow impacts, or incremental load growth. This

approach provides cost certainty and reduces speculative requests. Importantly, any such fee

must be calibrated so that it neither over-recovers costs from individual loads nor substitutes for

a rigorous assessment of actual system impacts. While the Commission may adopt an interim

value, a more deliberate long-term methodology should be developed.



                           VI.     SITE CONTROL REQUIREMENTS

       We support the Commission’s inclusion of purchase options as acceptable site control at

the Intermediate Agreement stage. We respectfully urge the Commission to extend this

flexibility to the Interconnection Agreement stage. Purchase and lease options are common

forms of site control during development. Purchasing land is expensive, binding, and typically

occurs only after financing is secured and interconnection costs are known. Requiring land

purchase before executing an Interconnection Agreement reverses the logical development

sequence and imposes unnecessary and premature financial exposure.

       ERCOT’s proposed study process allows only a 30-day window between final study

results and Interconnection Agreement execution. Because it is unreasonable to purchase land

before receiving study results, this timeline creates an impractical burden. Developers would be



                                                  8
 required to review results, make a go/no-go decision, exercise a purchase option, and execute the

Interconnection Agreement, all within 30 days. This compressed timeline is inconsistent with

standard development practices and creates avoidable commercial and financing risk.

       As an alternative, the Commission should allow a purchase option at the Interconnection

Agreement stage if the developer commits to converting the option into a purchase as a

contractual milestone. This approach maintains developer commitment while providing timing

flexibility aligned with standard development practices.



                              VII.    REGULATORY CERTAINTY

       Clarity is needed regarding how large load projects with an executed Interconnection

Agreement prior to adoption of the new rule will be treated. These projects should be exempt

from the batch study process and from posting new financial security requirements. Requiring

such projects to re-enter the process would be duplicative, costly, and inconsistent with

established investment expectations. Providing explicit grandfathering treatment will preserve

regulatory certainty and avoid undermining reliance interests for projects already well into

development.



                                       VIII. CONCLUSION

       APA and ACP appreciate the opportunity to provide comments in this project and look

forward to working with the Commission and market participants on these important matters.



Dated: April 17, 2026

                                             Respectfully submitted,

                                       PROJECT NO. 58481


    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                      §                  BEFORE THE
    LARGE LOAD                                   §          PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS                    §                   OF TEXAS
    UNDER PURA §37.0561


-    Texas is experiencing unprecedented growth in large, energy‑intensive industries, including
     data centers, advanced manufacturing, and other capital‑intensive facilities. As these sectors
     continue to expand, a predictable, commercially workable, and legally durable
     interconnection framework is essential to maintaining ERCOT system reliability and
     supporting continued economic development. The Commission’s Proposal for Publication
     represents an important step toward establishing such a framework, but several provisions
     require refinement to ensure alignment with PURA’s cost‑causation principles and the
     practical realities of large‑load development.

-    First, the proposed financial security structure imposes non‑refundable obligations at a stage
     when developers lack visibility into both MW allocation and upgrade cost responsibility. This
     premature capital exposure creates unnecessary financial risk and may deter otherwise viable
     projects. Security requirements should function as risk‑mitigation tools, not punitive fees,
     and should be tied to a developer’s actual, identifiable system impacts.

-    Second, the proposed treatment of Intermediate Agreements, particularly the application of
     subsection (g), risks forcing developers to forfeit substantial security before they have
     sufficient information to assess project viability. A more balanced approach would reduce
     initial security postings, limit non‑refundable components, and ensure that forfeitures occur
     only when a withdrawal imposes measurable costs on other requests in the cluster.

-    Third, the proposed site control requirements and execution timelines do not reflect standard
     development practices. Requiring land purchase before study results are known reverses the
     logical development sequence and introduces unnecessary financial exposure. Allowing
     purchase options at the Interconnection Agreement stage, coupled with a commitment to
     convert the option into ownership as a contractual milestone, preserves developer
     accountability while maintaining commercial feasibility.

-    Finally, regulatory certainty is essential. Projects that have already executed Interconnection
     Agreements under the existing framework should be grandfathered and exempt from new
     security postings or batch‑study requirements. Requiring such projects to re‑enter the process
     would be duplicative, costly, and inconsistent with established investment expectations.

With targeted refinements to the financial security structure, Intermediate Agreement provisions,
site control requirements, and grandfathering treatment, the Commission can adopt a durable,
transparent, and commercially reasonable standard that discourages speculation without
impeding the large‑load development critical to Texas’s continued economic leadership.

Agreement prior to adoption of the new rule will be treated. These proj ects should be exempt

from the batch study process and from posting new financial security requirements. Requiring

such projects to re-enter the process would be duplicative, costly, and inconsistent with

established investment expectations. Providing explicit grandfathering treatment will preserve

regulatory certainty and avoid undermining reliance interests for proj ects already well into

development.



                                       VIII. CONCLUSION

       APA and ACP appreciate the opportunity to provide comments in this project and look

forward to working with the Commission and market participants on these important matters.

                                        PROJECT NO. 58481


    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                       §                BEFORE THE
    LARGE LOAD                                    §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
    INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS                     §                 OF TEXAS
    UNDER PURA §37.0561


-    Texas is experiencing unprecedented growth in large, energy-intensive industries, including
     data centers, advanced manufacturing, and other capital-intensive facilities. As these sectors
     continue to expand, a predictable, commercially workable, and legally durable
     interconnection framework is essential to maintaining ERCOT system reliability and
     supporting continued economic development. The Commission's Proposal for Publication
     represents an important step toward establishing such a framework, but several provisions
     require refinement to ensure alignment with PURA's cost-causation principles and the
     practical realities of large-load development.

-    First, the proposed financial security structure imposes non-refundable obligations at a stage
     when developers lack visibility into both MW allocation and upgrade cost responsibility. This
     premature capital exposure creates unnecessary financial risk and may deter otherwise viable
     proj ects. Security requirements should function as risk-mitigation tools, not punitive fees,
     and should be tied to a developer's actual, identifiable system impacts.

-    Second, the proposed treatment of Intermediate Agreements, particularly the application of
     subsection (g), risks forcing developers to forfeit substantial security before they have
     sufficient information to assess project viability. A more balanced approach would reduce
     initial security postings, limit non-refundable components, and ensure that forfeitures occur
     only when a withdrawal imposes measurable costs on other requests in the cluster.

-    Third, the proposed site control requirements and execution timelines do not reflect standard
     development practices. Requiring land purchase before study results are known reverses the
     logical development sequence and introduces unnecessary financial exposure. Allowing
     purchase options at the Interconnection Agreement stage, coupled with a commitment to
     convert the option into ownership as a contractual milestone, preserves developer
     accountability while maintaining commercial feasibility.

-    Finally, regulatory certainty is essential. Projects that have already executed Interconnection
     Agreements under the existing framework should be grandfathered and exempt from new
     security postings or batch-study requirements. Requiring such proj ects to re-enter the process
     would be duplicative, costly, and inconsistent with established investment expectations.

With targeted refinements to the financial security structure, Intermediate Agreement provisions,
site control requirements, and grandfathering treatment, the Commission can adopt a durable,
transparent, and commercially reasonable standard that discourages speculation without
impeding the large-load development critical to Texas's continued economic leadership.
